hero.prompt: A friendly flat cartoon of a school laboratory bench holding a blue light microscope, a pot of clean cotton swabs, three glass slides, a small dropper bottle of blue stain, a box of cover slips and a closed grey bin beside the bench.
hero.alt: A school lab bench with a blue light microscope, cotton swabs, glass slides, a dropper bottle of blue stain, cover slips and a closed bin.

slides.title: Prediction Card: onion cell and your cheek cell
slides.subtitle: Think alone. Write quietly. No talking yet.
slides.time_note: SoW: 3 minutes of silent individual writing.

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph. It shows an onion cell like your Lesson 6 drawing.
Compared with the onion cell, I predict I will see ___ and I will NOT see ___, because ___.

do: Ask learners to take out their Lesson 6 annotated onion cell drawing and a Prediction Card (a small paper or a notebook page).
Show the Lesson 6 onion cell drawing on the board. Use a prepared exemplar or photograph a strong student drawing. The diagram on the slide can stand in.
Start the 3-minute timer. Enforce silence.
Circulate and scan 8 to 10 cards while learners write.
say: Before we touch any equipment, I want your brain to do some work. Look at your onion cell drawing. That was a PLANT cell.
You are about to look at YOUR OWN cell. That is an animal cell. I am about to look at a cell from the inside of my own cheek.
Finish two stems: I predict I WILL see… and I predict I will NOT see… Give a reason for each.
This is silent writing. Keep your ideas on paper for now.
notes.wait_time: 3 minutes of silent writing. Stay silent yourself.
look_for: Scan at least 8 to 10 cards for two things: (1) the learner names at least one plant-cell-only structure (cell wall, chloroplasts, large vacuole) as absent in the cheek cell; (2) the reason is about plant cell versus animal cell, not a guess.
Write down the names of learners who show neither. Question them more during the practical.
if_then: If a learner writes 'I don't know', say: 'Look at your onion drawing. Which labelled parts might an animal cell not have? Write one and tell me why you think so.'
If a learner starts talking, say: 'Hold that idea. Write it down first.'
If a learner has no onion drawing, say: 'Use the drawing on the screen to help you.'
notes.why_this_works: Retrieving what they saw in Lesson 6 gives every learner a starting point. When the cheek cell is different, the difference is easier to remember. Common misconception: every cell looks like the plant cell in textbooks.
answer_key: Model Prediction Card: 'I predict I will see a nucleus and cytoplasm, because every cell needs a control centre and a jelly-like inside. I predict I will NOT see a cell wall, chloroplasts or a large vacuole, because a cheek cell is an animal cell and those are plant cell structures.'

slides.title: Pair talk: agree and disagree
slides.subtitle: Share your Prediction Card with your shoulder partner.

items: check :: Find ONE thing you agree on
cross :: Find ONE thing you disagree on

blocks.text: Be ready to share. Four pairs will be asked.

do: Learners turn to their shoulder partner.
Start the 2-minute timer.
Listen in to three or four pairs. Note interesting agreements and disagreements.
say: Turn to your shoulder partner. You have 2 minutes.
Find ONE thing you agree on and ONE thing you disagree on.
Read your cards to each other. Give your reasons.
notes.wait_time: Stay quiet for the full 2 minutes.
notes.why_this_works: Saying a prediction aloud to one partner is safe practice before speaking to the class. Disagreement makes learners want to test the idea with the microscope.

slides.title: BEFORE — Our Predictions
slides.subtitle: Four pairs share. We do not say right or wrong yet.
slides.time_note: SoW: cold-call four pairs. The SoW gives no time, so 2 minutes is used.

blocks.text: Keep your Prediction Card. We will come back to it.

do: Copy the table onto the board under the heading BEFORE — Our Predictions.
Use the class register. Cold-call exactly 4 pairs: rows 1, 3, 5 and 7.
Ask each pair what they agreed on and what they disagreed on. Write it in the two columns.
Put a '?' next to any idea that may be wrong. Do not correct it.
say: Pair in row 1 — what did you AGREE on?
Now, what did you DISAGREE on?
Thank you. I will write that here. I am not saying right or wrong yet.
Keep your Prediction Card visible. We will come back to it the moment we finish observing. Scientists always test their own predictions.
notes.wait_time: 5 seconds after each question before you call on the pair.
look_for: Across the four pairs, at least two pairs predict that the cheek cell will NOT have a cell wall and give a plant versus animal reason.
Note any pair that disagrees about the same structure. Question that pair during the practical.
if_then: If a pair says 'we will see chloroplasts', say: 'Interesting. We will test that with our own eyes. I will put a question mark.'
If a pair has nothing to share, say: 'Tell me one thing your partner wrote that you did not.'
notes.why_this_works: Writing predictions in public with no corrections shows that scientists test ideas before they know the answer. The '?' marks give the class something to return to in Explain.

slides.title: Demonstration: make a cheek cell slide
slides.subtitle: Watch first. The teacher thinks aloud.
slides.time_note: SoW gives no time for the demonstration, so 4 minutes is used.

items: mouth :: Gently scrape inside your cheek with a clean swab.
blue_circle :: Smear it in a thin circle on a slide.
droplet :: Add ONE drop of methylene blue.
arrow_down :: Lower the cover slip at 45°.
hand :: Blot extra stain with tissue.
microscope :: Focus on ×4, then ×10, then ×40.

do: Do the demonstration at the front bench after the safety briefing. Use your own clean swab. Narrate every step aloud.
Hold the slide up so learners can see the thin smear.
Show how to lower the cover slip slowly at 45° so bubbles stay out.
Show the focus routine on the microscope: ×4 first, then ×10, then ×40.
Tell the class: each learner prepares their own slide, works in a pair, and records in their own book.
say: I scrape gently. I only need a few cells, not a lot.
I smear it in a thin circle. The smear should be thin enough to read newsprint through it. Too thick and you will not see single cells.
One drop of stain only. I will ask you what the stain is doing in a moment.
I lower the cover slip slowly at 45° so bubbles stay out.
I blot the extra stain with tissue. Now I put the slide on the stage and I start on the smallest power, ×4.
Look for single, flat cells at the edge of the smear. They will look pale and small.
if_then: If a demonstration slide has many bubbles, say: 'Bubbles are a problem. I will lower the cover slip more slowly next time.' Then remake it so learners see the fix.
If you cannot see cells, say: 'Not enough cells here. I will go back to ×4 and look at the edge of the smear.'
notes.why_this_works: A think-aloud lets learners hear the reasons behind each step, not only see the steps. They can then copy your decisions when their own slide is not perfect.
notes.science_note: Cheek cells are thin and flat. With school microscopes they look pale blue with a darker round nucleus. Cells often overlap, and some slides will be hard to read. Tell learners that honest, faint results are valid evidence.

slides.title: Your turn: prepare, focus and draw
slides.subtitle: One swab each. Draw only what you can see.
slides.time_note: SoW: 25 minutes for slide preparation, focusing and drawing. Trimmed to 20 so the lesson fits 80 minutes.

blocks.text: Work in pairs. Each of you makes your own slide.

items: pencil :: Pencil drawing, at least 5 cm across
ruler :: Ruled label lines for every structure you can see
magnifier :: Write the magnification and the date
handshake :: Partner checks your drawing

blocks.text: Label only what you can positively identify.

do: Pairs at bench stations. Hand out the printed protocol card, one clean swab per learner, slides, cover slips, methylene blue and a microscope for each pair.
Each learner makes their own slide, then draws in the drawing box in their notebook.
Start the 20-minute timer. Circulate all the time.

At each station ask one question. Rotate through: 'What is the blue stain doing to the cell?', 'Why can you see the nucleus more clearly now?', 'What structure would you expect to see in the onion cell that you do NOT see here?'
At the 15-minute mark say the time warning.
Partner checks the drawing against the slide. Then the slide is disposed of safely.
Keep a Drawing Checklist Clipboard: a grid with learner names. Tick for each pair.
say: Every learner makes their own slide. One swab each. No sharing.
Used swabs go straight into the bleach bin.
Five minutes remaining for your drawing. Make sure every structure you can see has a label line.
Show me on your slide what you are drawing.
look_for: Check every pair with the clipboard: (1) the drawing is at least 5 cm, in pencil, with smooth outlines and no shading; (2) at least three structures are labelled (cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus at minimum); (3) the magnification is written; (4) NO cell wall is labelled on the cheek cell.
Note any learner who cannot say why there is no cell wall. Follow up in the Explain phase.
if_then: If a learner has labelled a cell wall on the cheek cell, stop and say: 'Show me the cell wall on your slide right now under the microscope.'
If a pair cannot find any cells, say: 'Go back to ×4. Look at the thinnest edge of your smear, not the middle.'
If a slide breaks, say: 'Hands OFF. Call me.' The teacher cleans up with a dustpan.
If a learner has an open sore or an oral infection, give them the role of data recorder and drawing checker.
notes.why_this_works: A drawing makes a learner decide what is really there and what is not. Labelling only what they can see stops them copying the plant cell from memory. Common misconception: animal cells have a cell wall like the onion cell.
answer_key: Model drawing: a large pencil drawing (at least 5 cm) of ONE cheek cell with a smooth outline. Label lines are ruled and do not cross. Labels: nucleus (a darker round part inside the cell), cytoplasm (the pale material around the nucleus), cell membrane (the outer edge). A title: Human cheek cell. Magnification written, for example ×400 if the eyepiece is ×10 and the objective is ×40. Date written. No cell wall labelled.
notes.science_note: Honest results are valid evidence. Many cheek cell slides show faint cells with overlapping edges. Praise learners who draw what they see rather than what they expect.

slides.title: Compare: onion cell and cheek cell
slides.subtitle: Put your Lesson 6 drawing beside today's drawing.
slides.time_note: SoW gives no time for the evidence table. 5 minutes used.

blocks.text: List every structure you saw. ✓ = in both cells. ★ = in one cell only.

do: Learners put the cheek cell drawing next to the Lesson 6 onion cell drawing.
Learners copy the two-column table into their notebooks and fill it in alone.
Circulate. Read the cheek cell column in 8 notebooks.
say: Put today's drawing next to your onion drawing.
List every structure you actually saw. Put a tick on structures that are in both cells. Put a star on structures in one cell only.
Use only what you saw, not what a textbook says.
The cell membrane is in the onion cell too. We just did not label it in Lesson 6. So it gets a tick.
notes.wait_time: Let learners work for the full time. Stay quiet for the first minute.
look_for: Check 8 notebooks: the cheek cell column does not list a cell wall, and the onion cell column lists a cell wall.
Each learner can point to at least two differences they actually saw (for example cell wall and large vacuole present only in onion).
Ticks mark nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane (in both cells); stars mark the cell wall and the large vacuole (onion only).
if_then: If a learner lists a cell wall for the cheek cell, say: 'Look at your drawing. Where is the cell wall? Show me on your slide.'
If a learner lists structures they did not see, say: 'Did you see that or read it? Only write what you saw.'
If a learner has no ticks, say: 'Which structures did both cells have? Draw a tick next to each.'
If a learner gives the cell membrane a star as a cheek-only structure, say: 'Every cell has a membrane, plant cells too. In the onion cell it sits just inside the wall. Which symbol does it need?'
notes.why_this_works: Putting two drawings side by side turns two separate observations into comparative evidence. That is the main move needed for the driving question. Common misconception: animal cells have a cell wall like the onion cell.
answer_key: ONION CELL (plant): cell wall ★, large vacuole ★, nucleus ✓, cytoplasm ✓, cell membrane ✓ (inside the wall; not labelled on the Lesson 6 drawing).
CHEEK CELL (animal): nucleus ✓, cytoplasm ✓, cell membrane ✓. No cell wall, no large vacuole.
Two observed differences: the onion cell has a cell wall and a large vacuole; the cheek cell does not.

slides.title: Check your Prediction Cards
slides.subtitle: Use a different colour pen.
slides.time_note: SoW says come back to the card after observing. The SoW gives no time, so 2 minutes is used.

items: eyes :: Read your Prediction Card again.
pencil :: With a different colour pen, tick what you got right.
cross :: Cross what was wrong. Do not rub anything out.

do: Learners take out their Prediction Cards and a pen of a different colour.
Point to the BEFORE — Our Predictions list on the board with the '?' marks.
Give 2 minutes. Walk round and look at 5 cards.
say: Look at your Prediction Card. It is time to test it.
Use a different colour pen. Tick what you predicted correctly. Cross what was wrong.
Being wrong is useful. It tells us something new.
notes.why_this_works: Marking predictions in a different colour shows learners how their thinking changed. It makes being wrong a normal part of science.
answer_key: Model marked card: 'I predict I will see a nucleus and cytoplasm ✓. I predict I will NOT see a cell wall, chloroplasts or a large vacuole ✓ — I did not see them in my cheek cell.'

slides.title: Evidence Harvest: our T-chart
slides.subtitle: One observation from each pair.
slides.time_note: SoW: Evidence Harvest 10 minutes in total, T-chart 6 to 7 minutes. Trimmed to 5.

blocks.text: What is ONE thing you actually SAW? Not something from the textbook.

do: Draw the T-chart on the board with the three headings.
Go round the room, one pair per turn. Each pair gives ONE observation from their table.
Write each item in the right column.
Keep going until the chart is full. Do not repeat items.
say: I need one observation from your table — something you actually SAW, not something from the textbook.
Which column does it go in?
Does anyone have something different to add?
The cell membrane is in the onion cell too. We just did not label it in Lesson 6. So it goes in PRESENT IN BOTH.
notes.wait_time: 5 seconds after each pair is called.
look_for: Every pair gives an observation that matches their own table.
The ONLY IN PLANT CELL column includes the cell wall and the large vacuole.
The cell membrane, nucleus and cytoplasm are in PRESENT IN BOTH, not in the animal column.
No pair adds a structure they did not see.
if_then: If a pair gives a textbook item such as mitochondria, say: 'Show me that on your drawing. Did you see it today?'
If a learner says chloroplasts, say: 'Think about Lesson 6. Did we see chloroplasts in the onion skin cells? Why not?'
If a pair repeats an item, say: 'Good. Now look at your table and find something different.'
If a pair puts the cell membrane under ONLY IN ANIMAL CELL, say: 'The onion cell has a membrane too, just inside the wall. We did not label it in Lesson 6. Which column does it belong in?'
notes.why_this_works: A shared chart turns 30 separate drawings into one body of class evidence. Asking for what learners SAW keeps the evidence separate from what they have read.
answer_key: PRESENT IN BOTH: nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane.
ONLY IN PLANT CELL (onion): cell wall, large vacuole.

ONLY IN ANIMAL CELL (cheek): expect this column to be empty or very short. Every structure learners saw in the cheek cell is also in the onion cell. An empty column is a result in itself. Learners may add the irregular shape of the cheek cell (no wall), but this is a feature, not a structure.

slides.title: What do the differences mean?
slides.subtitle: Look at the T-chart. Think about what each structure does.
slides.time_note: SoW gives no time for these questions. 3 minutes used, with 3 more on the next slide.

items: thinking :: Plant column: what do these have in common in function?
question :: Animal column: what does having no rigid wall allow a cell to do?

do: Ask the two questions one at a time. Reveal one question each time.

Question 1: ask about the ONLY IN PLANT CELL column. Wait 12 seconds in silence. Cold-call 3 learners: pick one who predicted no cell wall, one who marked a prediction wrong, and one who has not spoken yet.
Question 2: ask about the ONLY IN ANIMAL CELL column, or what is NOT there. Wait 10 seconds. Cold-call 2 learners.
say: Look at the ONLY IN PLANT CELL column. Every item in that column — what do they all have in common in terms of function?
Now look at the ONLY IN ANIMAL CELL column, or notice what is NOT there. What does the absence of a rigid cell wall allow an animal cell to do that a plant cell cannot easily do?
notes.wait_time: 12 seconds after question 1. 10 seconds after question 2.
look_for: Listen to at least 5 answers. Do learners link plant-only structures to a plant that stays in one place?
Do learners say that having no wall lets an animal cell be flexible or change shape?
if_then: If a learner says 'plants need them', say: 'What do they need them for? What does the cell wall do for a plant that cannot move?'
If a learner says 'animal cells are softer', say: 'Good start. What can a soft cell do that a rigid cell cannot?'
notes.why_this_works: A chain of small questions leads learners to build the idea themselves from their own evidence. The idea of flexibility is named only after they have found it. Misconception addressed: animal cells have a wall like plant cells.
answer_key: Question 1: the plant-only structures all relate to the plant's fixed, non-moving lifestyle.
Question 2: with no rigid wall, an animal cell can change shape, so it is flexible.

slides.title: Link to the healing cut
slides.subtitle: Think about the clot on the cut finger.
slides.time_note: SoW gives no time for this link. 3 minutes used.

blocks.text: A girl smiling and holding up one finger with a neat plaster on it, beside a chopping board with sliced onions.
items: amina_healing_finger

A friendly flat cartoon of one teenage girl in a school uniform smiling and holding up one hand with a neat plaster on her finger, standing beside a kitchen table with a wooden chopping board of sliced onions.

blocks.text: Could Aisha's platelets change shape if they had a rigid cell wall?

do: Ask the question. Learners talk to their partner for 30 seconds.
Cold-call one pair. Choose a pair who have not spoken yet.
Listen to at least 4 pairs as they talk.
say: Remember Aisha's platelets — tiny, irregular animal cells that flatten and extend pseudopods to patch the wound. Could they do that if they had a rigid cell wall? Turn and tell your partner — 30 seconds.
look_for: Listen to at least 4 pairs. Do they link having no wall to being flexible and to platelets changing shape in the healing cut?
if_then: If no pair links to platelets, say: 'Think about the clot on the cut finger. The platelets must change shape. Does a rigid wall help or stop that?'
If a pair says 'yes, they could', say: 'What did your cheek cell have around it? Did you see a wall? What does a wall do to shape?'
notes.why_this_works: Returning to the cut finger shows that what students saw under the microscope helps explain a real event. Misconception addressed: animal cells have a wall like plant cells.
answer_key: No. A rigid wall would stop the platelets changing shape to patch the wound.

slides.title: Write your explanation
slides.subtitle: Three sentences, then one sentence about Aisha's finger.
slides.time_note: SoW gives no time for the writing. 5 minutes used.

blocks.text: Write 3 sentences: what differences between plant and animal cells did you see? What might having no cell wall mean for an animal cell?
items: Finish: When the platelets in Aisha's cut finger change shape to form a clot, this is possible because animal cells…

do: Learners write alone in their notebooks.
Circulate and read over shoulders. Read 4 to 5 responses. Do not collect yet.
At the end, collect the notebooks or take photos of the explanations as an exit indicator.
say: Write three sentences in your notebook. Use the words cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, cell wall and flexible.
Then finish the sentence about Aisha's finger.
Use what you saw today as your evidence.
look_for: Read 4 to 5 responses as learners write. Each should have (1) at least two structures named with correct words, (2) the word flexible or an equivalent such as 'can change shape' or 'no rigid wall', (3) a phenomenon sentence that links no cell wall to platelet function or animal cell movement.
Learners who meet all three are ready. Learners who meet one or none get a prompt card at the Driving Question Board.
if_then: If a learner writes only 'animal cells have no wall', say: 'Why does that matter? What can the cell do because of it?'
If a learner cannot start, say: 'Begin with: Under the microscope I saw…'
If a learner meets one marker or none, give the prompt card: 'Go back to your T-chart. Which column has cell wall? Is a cheek cell in that column?'
notes.why_this_works: Moving from 'I saw this' to 'this tells us something about how cells work' is the key thinking skill in the unit. The phenomenon sentence closes the loop from prediction to evidence to explanation.
answer_key: 'Under the microscope I saw a nucleus and cytoplasm in both the onion cell and the cheek cell. The onion cell also had a cell wall and a large vacuole, but I could not see a cell wall in the cheek cell. With no rigid cell wall, an animal cell is flexible and can change shape.'
'When the platelets in Aisha's cut finger change shape to form a clot, this is possible because animal cells have no rigid cell wall, so they can be flexible and change shape.'

slides.title: Write your Evidence Card
slides.subtitle: Use something you saw today. Silent writing.

blocks.text: A classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes with small gold stars beside some of them.
items: dqb_sticky_notes_board
A friendly flat cartoon of a classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes, with three small gold stars stuck beside some notes, and a wooden desk with a pot of pencils in front.

blocks.text: Write ONE Evidence Card. Post it under Lesson 7 Evidence.
items: We observed that animal cells have no cell wall — this tells us…

do: Give each learner a sticky note or index card.
Point to the Driving Question Board and the section labelled Lesson 7 Evidence.
Start the 3-minute timer. Enforce silence.
Learners post their cards on the Driving Question Board when finished.
say: This is YOUR thinking. No copying from the board yet.
Finish the sentence on the slide. Use something you saw today, not something from a book.
When you finish, post your card under Lesson 7 Evidence.
look_for: Read 6 to 8 cards as learners post. Sort them in your head into three tiers: Tier 1 restates the observation; Tier 2 makes an inference; Tier 3 links to the phenomenon.
Aim for at least half of the cards to be Tier 2 or 3. Note learners with only Tier 1 cards for small-group talk at the start of Lesson 8.
if_then: If a learner writes only 'we saw no cell wall', say: 'Good observation. Now finish the sentence: this tells us…'
If a learner copies from the board, say: 'Close your eyes. What did you see in your cheek cell? Write that.'
If a learner is stuck, give the prompt card: 'Go back to your T-chart. Which column has cell wall? Is a cheek cell in that column?'
notes.why_this_works: Cards built from today's observations keep the board an evidence record, not a copy of the textbook. The sentence frame moves learners from what they saw to what it tells us.
answer_key: Tier 1: 'We saw no cell wall in the cheek cell.'
Tier 2: 'This tells us animal cells can be more flexible.'
Tier 3: 'This tells us platelets can change shape to plug Aisha's wound because they have no rigid wall.'

slides.title: Walk the Driving Question Board
slides.subtitle: Read the cards. Tick the ones that teach you something new.

items: eyes :: Read at least two cards that are NOT yours
check :: Tick a card that adds an idea you did not write

do: Learners walk to the Driving Question Board in small streams to avoid crowding.
Give each learner a pencil or a pen to make a small tick.
Start the 2-minute timer.
say: Walk the board. Read at least two cards that are NOT yours.
Put a small tick on any card that teaches you something new.
notes.why_this_works: Reading and ticking classmates' cards makes learners compare ideas. Ideas that appear on several ticked cards become visible to the whole class.

slides.title: What does our evidence tell us?
slides.subtitle: Think about the driving question.
slides.time_note: SoW: 5 minutes of debrief. Trimmed to 3.

blocks.text: Which card most directly answers part of our driving question?

items: raised_hand :: Vote: can we answer it fully, partly or not yet?
question :: What NEW question does today's evidence raise?

do: Cold-call 3 learners to nominate a card and say why. Choose one learner whose card was ticked often, one who wrote a Tier 3 card, and one who has not spoken yet.
Ask for new questions. Write them on the Driving Question Board under a strip labelled NEW QUESTIONS — Lesson 7.
Point to the driving question at the top of the board: Why do cells in our body look so different from each other — and how does the shape of a cell determine the job it can do?
Hold the class vote by hands: fully, partly, or not yet. Count the hands and write the count on the board.
Photograph the Driving Question Board after the lesson for tier analysis.
say: Which card on this board most directly answers part of our driving question? Why did you choose it?
What NEW question does today's evidence raise that we have not yet answered?
These are exactly the questions a biologist would ask. We will need more evidence to answer them.
Can we answer our driving question yet — fully, partly, or not yet? Hands up for each.
look_for: Listen to the 3 learners. Do they point to a card that uses something seen today?
Count the vote. Most learners should vote 'partly'. If many vote 'fully', ask which piece of the puzzle is still missing.
Count how many new questions are raised.
if_then: If a learner picks a card with no evidence, say: 'What did you see today that supports this card?'
If many learners vote 'fully', say: 'We know something about wall-free cells. Do we know why a red blood cell has the shape it has yet?'
If no new questions come, say: 'What can't your drawing of the animal cell explain yet?'
notes.why_this_works: A vote and a named gap show learners that science answers questions in pieces. Naming new questions keeps curiosity alive between lessons.
answer_key: Example new questions: 'If animal cells have no wall, what stops them from bursting?', 'Do all animal cells look like cheek cells?', 'Why does the nucleus look darker in some cells?'
Expected vote: partly answered. The full answer needs the specialisation lessons.

slides.title: Model: draw the animal cell
slides.subtitle: Add it next to your plant cell. Use a NEW colour.
slides.time_note: SoW: 8 minutes to draw and annotate in total. Trimmed to 6 across two slides.

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph. Check your own drawing against it.

items: book :: Open your Cell Structure Model page.
pencil :: Draw the animal cell next to your plant cell, about the same size.

do: Learners open the cumulative Cell Structure Model page they have built since Lesson 1.
Learners draw the animal cell next to the plant cell with a new colour pen or pencil.
Circulate. Check 8 models for: (1) animal cell drawn with NO cell wall; (2) nucleus drawn as a distinct structure inside the cytoplasm; (3) ruled, horizontal label lines.
say: Open to your Cell Structure Model page. You have been building this since Lesson 1.
Today you are adding the animal cell. Draw it next to your plant cell. Make them roughly the same size so we can compare directly.
Use a NEW colour for today's changes.
look_for: Check 8 models: no cell wall on the animal cell (PASS or FAIL). Note every FAIL for the start of Lesson 8.
At least three structures labelled on the animal cell.
Label lines ruled and horizontal.
if_then: If a learner draws a cell wall on the animal cell, say: 'Look at your cheek cell drawing from today. Did you see a cell wall there? Redraw it.'
If the animal cell is much bigger or smaller than the plant cell, say: 'Make them roughly the same size so we can compare directly.'
If a learner has no plant cell drawing, give them 30 seconds to copy it from a partner.
notes.why_this_works: Adding to one model each lesson makes learning progress visible. Learners see what is new and what stays the same. Misconception addressed: animal cells have a cell wall.
answer_key: Model page: plant cell on the left from earlier lessons. New animal cell drawn in a new colour, with a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus labelled, and no cell wall.

slides.title: Model: link and explain
slides.subtitle: Show what is the same and what is missing.
slides.time_note: Second part of the SoW's 8 minutes of drawing and annotation.

items: arrow_right :: Draw arrows between matching structures. Example: nucleus ↔ nucleus.
pencil :: Next to each structure the animal cell does NOT have, write what it does in the plant cell.
palette :: Use your new colour.

blocks.text: Add this line to your model page:
items: This model is based on evidence from…

do: Learners draw arrows between matching structures in the two diagrams.
Learners write one sentence next to each structure that is absent in the animal cell.
Circulate and read 6 model pages.
say: Draw arrows between matching structures. Nucleus to nucleus is one example.
Next to each structure that the animal cell does NOT have, write one sentence. What does that structure do in the plant cell?
Finish with: This model is based on evidence from… Say what you saw today.
look_for: Check 6 model pages: arrows join nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane.
At least two 'absent structure' sentences correctly link the missing structure to its plant-cell function.
The evidence line names today's cheek cell observation.
if_then: If a learner writes 'it has no cell wall' only, say: 'What does a cell wall do for the plant cell? Write that.'
If a learner draws arrows for structures that are missing, say: 'An arrow joins two structures that both exist. Which ones are in both cells?'
If a learner leaves the evidence line blank, say: 'What did you actually see under the microscope today? Write that.'
notes.why_this_works: Linking the two cells and writing what is missing makes learners compare structure and function. Citing evidence keeps the model tied to observations, not memory.
answer_key: Arrows: nucleus ↔ nucleus, cytoplasm ↔ cytoplasm, cell membrane ↔ cell membrane.
Cell wall: gives the plant cell a strong, fixed shape and support.
Chloroplast: makes food for the plant by photosynthesis, using light.
Large central vacuole: stores water and helps keep the plant cell firm.
'This model is based on evidence from the cheek cells and onion cells I observed under the microscope.'

slides.title: Model Update Statement
slides.subtitle: What does your model show? What can it not explain yet?
slides.time_note: SoW: Model Update Statement and cold-calls, no times given. 5 minutes used.

blocks.text: Write two sentences at the bottom of your model page.
items: My model now shows… but does not yet explain…
Next lesson I predict…

do: Learners write the Model Update Statement and a one-sentence prediction for the next lesson.
Cold-call 3 learners to read their 'does not yet explain' clause aloud. Choose one with a specific gap, one with a vague gap, and one who has not spoken yet.
Write their gaps on the board under Open Questions for Our Model.
Collect or photograph the model pages at the end of the lesson.
say: Write: My model now shows… but does not yet explain…
The second part is just as important as the first. A scientist who knows what their model CANNOT explain yet is a scientist who knows what to investigate next.
Now write one sentence: Next lesson I predict…

You have just looked at your own cells under a microscope — the same type of cell that lines the inside of the wound when Aisha cut her finger. Next lesson, we ask: if all these cells started the same way, how did they end up so different?
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds after asking each learner to read.
look_for: Check 8 to 10 model pages with these four criteria: (1) animal cell drawn with no cell wall, PASS or FAIL; (2) at least three structures labelled; (3) at least two absent-structure sentences correct; (4) the 'does not yet explain' clause names a specific gap.
Failures on criterion 1 need action at the start of Lesson 8. Use criteria 3 and 4 to plan Lesson 8 groups.
if_then: If a learner writes 'does not yet explain everything', say: 'Be more specific. What exactly can your model not explain? Think about a cell in blood.'
If the next-lesson prediction is blank, say: 'Think about the cells in a cut finger. Will they all look the same? Write what you think.'
If a learner's model has a cell wall on the animal cell, say: 'Go back to your cheek drawing and fix this now.'
notes.why_this_works: Naming what a model cannot yet explain trains learners to see the limits of what they know. This becomes the next question for investigation and keeps the unit story moving.
answer_key: 'My model now shows an animal cell with a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus but no cell wall, but does not yet explain why red blood cells have no nucleus.'
'Next lesson I predict that blood cells will have different shapes from cheek cells because they do different jobs.'

build_log.sow_says: T-chart: PRESENT IN BOTH | ONLY IN PLANT CELL (onion) | ONLY IN ANIMAL CELL (cheek); learners label 'cell membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus' on the cheek cell and 'cell wall, vacuole, and nucleus' on the onion cell (Lesson 6).
build_log.deck_does: Puts cell membrane, nucleus and cytoplasm under PRESENT IN BOTH in the answer key and adds a teacher line that the membrane is in the onion cell too and was not labelled in Lesson 6. The ONLY IN ANIMAL CELL column is expected to be empty or very short.
build_log.why: A cell membrane is present in onion cells too. The Lesson 6 onion drawing does not label it, so a learner's tables could place it as animal-only. The SoW owner should add the cell membrane to the Lesson 6 onion drawing labels or explain this.

build_log.slide: Compare: onion cell and cheek cell
build_log.sow_says: List every structure under each column, marking shared structures with a tick and unique structures with a star; cheek cell labels: cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus; onion cell labels in Lesson 6: cell wall, vacuole, nucleus.
build_log.deck_does: The answer key gives the cell membrane a tick in both columns and tells the teacher to say so. The ONION CELL answer notes that the membrane sits inside the wall and was not labelled in Lesson 6.
build_log.why: Same issue as the T-chart. The key must match so the teacher does not mark the membrane as a cheek-only structure.

build_log.sow_says: Learners label every structure they can positively identify, including 'cell membrane' on the cheek cell drawing.
build_log.deck_does: Keeps the cell membrane as a required label on the slide and in the notes, as the SoW says.
build_log.why: With a school light microscope the membrane is very thin and is not seen as a separate structure; learners see only the cell edge. Teacher to check whether the membrane should be a required label.

build_log.sow_says: 'Remember Aisha's platelets — tiny, irregular animal cells that flatten and extend pseudopods to patch the wound.'
build_log.deck_does: Uses the SoW words unchanged in the SAY line and on the slide.
build_log.why: Platelets are cell fragments without a nucleus, not whole cells, so they are not 'animal cells' in the same way as cheek cells. Platelet 'pseudopods' is also an odd term. Teacher to check.

build_log.sow_says: 'Guide toward the answer that plant-specific structures (cell wall, large vacuole, chloroplasts) are all related to the plant's fixed, non-moving lifestyle.'
build_log.deck_does: Keeps this as the expected answer in the answer key.
build_log.why: Chloroplasts and the vacuole relate to making food and storing water, not directly to being fixed in place. The claim is over-simple. Teacher to check.

lesson_oneliner: Look at your own cheek cells under the microscope and compare them with onion cells.
purpose: Learners prepare a slide of their own cheek cells, focus a light microscope and draw what they see.
They place the cheek cell drawing beside the Lesson 6 onion cell drawing and find at least two differences they actually saw.

Why it matters: this is their first first-hand look at an animal cell. A cell with no rigid wall can change shape. This links to platelets and epidermal cells in the healing cut and to the driving question.
Most important misconception to catch: learners label a cell wall on the cheek cell because they copy the onion cell from memory.
before_class: Prepare the 1% bleach solution and put it in a closed bin before class.
Check every microscope: lenses clean, light working, ×4, ×10 and ×40 objectives present.
Set out clean cotton swabs (one per learner), glass slides, cover slips, methylene blue with droppers, tissue and a dustpan.
Prepare an exemplar of the Lesson 6 onion cell drawing, or photograph a strong learner drawing.
Make the Drawing Checklist Clipboard: a grid of learner names with the four drawing checks.
Prepare the Driving Question Board with a section labelled Lesson 7 Evidence and a strip labelled NEW QUESTIONS — Lesson 7.
Have sticky notes or index cards ready, and a pen of a different colour for each learner.
Identify learners with an open sore or an oral infection. Give them the data recorder role.
Make one practice cheek cell slide yourself so your demonstration runs smoothly.
do_not_show: Do not show the slide 'Model: draw the animal cell' until learners have finished their own cheek cell drawings. It carries a labelled cheek cell diagram.
Do not show or play any ARES video or reading that compares plant and animal cells until the T-chart is complete.
Keep the answer keys in these notes private. Do not show a completed T-chart or comparison table before learners give their own observations.
so_far: You have met cells, compared plant and animal cell diagrams, and drawn onion cells under the microscope.
goals: Prepare a slide of your cheek cells and observe it with a microscope.
Draw and label the structures you can see in a cheek cell.
Compare cheek cells with onion cells and explain what the differences might mean.

key_words.definition: A temporary slide. The sample sits in a drop of liquid under a thin cover slip.
A coloured liquid that makes parts of a cell easier to see.
How many times bigger the microscope makes the image look.
A clear pencil drawing of what you see, with ruled label lines.
What you actually see or measure, not what you have read.

safety.title: Safety first
rules: One clean swab each. Never share a swab.
Put used swabs straight into the closed bleach bin.
Methylene blue can irritate. Keep it off your eyes and skin. Wash your hands after.
Glass breaks. If a slide breaks, hands OFF and call your teacher.
Open sore or mouth infection? Tell your teacher. You will be the recorder.

do: Stand at the front bench with the bleach bin, a swab, a slide, the stain bottle and the dustpan visible.
Read the five rules one at a time. Point to each item as you say the rule.
Show the closed bin and say it holds 1% bleach prepared in advance.
Remind learners with an open sore or oral infection to tell you quietly. Give them the data recorder and drawing checker role.
Keep to three minutes. Then go straight to the demonstration.
say: Three things matter most today. One swab per person, with no sharing. Used swabs go straight into the bleach bin, not on the bench. If a slide breaks, hands OFF and call me.
Methylene blue is a mild irritant. Keep it off your eyes and skin. Wash your hands well when we finish.
If you have an open sore or a mouth infection, tell me now. You will have an important job as recorder.
I sweep up broken glass with a dustpan. You never pick it up with bare hands.
notes.why_this_works: A few clear rules tied to real objects are easier to remember than a long list. Giving learners who cannot take part a real job keeps everyone in the lesson.

rows.what: Unit map, goals and safety briefing
Prediction Card, pair talk, four pairs share (BEFORE)
Teacher demonstration, then make slide, focus and draw cheek cell
Compare onion and cheek drawings in a two-column table
Mark predictions, T-chart, questions, link to cut, write explanation
Evidence Cards, gallery walk, debrief and class vote
Draw animal cell, link to plant cell, Model Update Statement
Summary Table at the end or as homework

materials: Clean cotton swab: one per learner, never shared
Clean glass slide and cover slip for each learner
Compound light microscope at each pair's bench station
Tissue for blotting; printed protocol card
Closed bin with 1% bleach solution, made in advance
Dustpan; pencils, rulers, pens of a different colour
Lesson 6 onion drawings; sticky notes or index cards
glance.fallback: If microscopes are short, pairs share one microscope in turns while partners draw. If still short, show one cheek cell slide at the front as a teacher demonstration, then learners draw from it. Label it clearly.

resource_notes.note: Explains plant versus animal cell differences, which students should predict first. Show after the 'Check your Prediction Cards' slide, or after the Evidence Harvest T-chart.
Plant versus animal exercise would give the answers away before the practical. Use as practice after 'Evidence Harvest: our T-chart' or as revision after Explain.
Prokaryote versus eukaryote content belongs to Lesson 3, not today's plant versus animal comparison. Use only as brief revision after the Model slides.
Cell membrane reading links to the flexibility idea. Check the depth, as fluid mosaic detail may be too much. Use after 'What do the differences mean?'
Membrane overview may help with the 'what stops cells bursting?' question. Preview its depth and pace for Grade 10 before showing it after the DQB walk.
Membrane practice questions go beyond today's evidence cards. Use as revision after the 'Model Update Statement' slide, or when the bursting question is followed up in Lesson 8.
Covers many organelles that students did not see in cheek cells. Check it supports the simple animal cell model; consider showing only the nucleus and membrane parts.
Membrane exercise is more detailed than today's model needs. Use as follow-up practice after the 'Model Update Statement' slide, or in Lesson 8.

summary.observe_prompt: Say how you made your slide and what you saw in your cheek cells.
summary.learn_prompt: Write which structures cheek cells have and which onion cell structures they do not.
summary.explain_prompt: Link having no cell wall to platelets changing shape in the healing cut.
summary.next_lesson: Why do blood cells and skin cells look so different if they all started the same way?
summary.answer_observe: I made a wet mount of my own cheek cells with methylene blue stain and focused it under the light microscope. I drew a labelled cheek cell. I saw a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus.
summary.answer_learn: Animal cells such as cheek cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus. They have no cell wall, chloroplasts or large central vacuole. The onion cells in Lesson 6 had a cell wall and a large vacuole. With no rigid wall, animal cells can be flexible and irregular in shape.
summary.answer_explain: The differences between plant and animal cells are not random. They match what each cell needs to do. With no cell wall, an animal cell can change shape. Cells such as platelets and epidermal cells can flatten, extend and move to close the wound in the cut finger because no rigid wall holds them in place. This is one piece of the puzzle of how cell shape fits cell job.
reflection: Did every learner use the bleach bin correctly? Were any swabs shared or glass handled unsafely? Were learners who could not take part given a meaningful role? What will I change in the next safety briefing?
How many drawings met the standard: large, in pencil, labelled, magnification recorded? Which part of the technique was weakest?
Did any learner label a cell wall on the cheek cell? How many? Did my questions at the bench fix it, or do I need a comparison task at the start of Lesson 8?
What share of Evidence Cards were Tier 2 or 3? What does this tell me about readiness for cell specialisation?
Did learners link having no cell wall to platelets changing shape by themselves, or did they need a lot of help? Should I retell the healing cut story at the start of Lesson 8?

do: Show the Summary Table. Learners answer the three questions in their notebooks, alone.
Do it at the end of the lesson or as homework.
Read 4 to 5 answers. Check that the cheek cell answers use what learners saw, and that the third answer links to the cut finger.
say: What did you observe today? Write only what you saw.
What did you learn about cheek cells, compared with onion cells?
How does this help explain the healing cut? Think about platelets and Aisha's finger.
notes.why_this_works: Writing three linked answers moves learners from what they saw to what it means, and back to the cut finger. This closes the predict, observe and explain loop.

do: Show the unit map. Point to YOU ARE HERE at Lesson 7.
Read the So far line aloud.
Read the unit driving question from the board or slide.
Keep it to one minute.
say: Last lesson you looked at onion cells under the microscope. Today you look at a cell from your own body.
Our big question is still: why do cells in our body look so different from each other, and how does the shape of a cell decide its job?
Today's evidence will be one more piece of that puzzle.
unit_map_notes.why_this_works: Showing where today sits in the unit helps learners see the lesson as one step in a story. Returning to the driving question keeps the healing cut in mind.

do: Read the three goals aloud.
Read the five key words with their plain meanings.
Do not ask for answers yet. Tell learners they will use these words during the practical.
say: By the end of today you can prepare a slide, draw what you see, and compare two kinds of cell.
These words will help you today. A wet mount is a temporary slide. A stain makes cells easier to see. Magnification tells us how much bigger the image looks.
Evidence means what you actually see. Use only evidence today.
goals_notes.why_this_works: A short look at the goals and the words before the work lets learners know what success looks like. Words that describe the method will not give away what they will see.
